cards.advice: When a routine starts slipping, a specific when-and-where plan helps more than trying harder, and a fresh one can help when the current one stopped working.
cards.action: Write the plan as a time and a place, such as 7:00 AM at the gym on the way to work; if it already has both, try a different pair for two weeks.

evidence.claim: Across 94 tests, people who planned when, where and how to act reached their goals more often than people who only intended to.
evidence.quote: Findings from 94 independent tests showed that implementation intentions had a positive effect of medium‐to‐large magnitude ( d = .65) on goal attainment.

cards.limitation: Most studies were short and many were lab tasks; the effect in a busy everyday routine may be smaller. The review did not test changing an existing plan.
quip_seeds: {behavior} went from {baseline_rate_pct} to {recent_rate_pct}. A specific when-and-where plan, like a set time just after something you already do, may help.
{behavior} went from {baseline_rate_pct} to {recent_rate_pct}. A specific when and where, such as a time and the place you will be, may help.

cards.advice: Name the obstacle that keeps getting in the way, and decide now what you will do when it shows up.
cards.action: Write the usual obstacle and your fallback in the Behavior's description, where you will see it next time.

evidence.claim: Picturing the goal, naming the obstacle and planning a response (mental contrasting with implementation intentions) helped people reach goals, with a small to medium effect.
evidence.quote: Results showed that MCII to be effective for goal attainment with a small to medium effect size (g = 0.336).

cards.limitation: The effect is small to moderate and, because of publication bias, may be smaller than reported.
quip_seeds: {behavior} dropped from {baseline_rate_pct} to {recent_rate_pct} over {recent_days|day|days}. What usually gets in the way?
{behavior}: {recent_completed} of {recent_resolved} lately. What gets in the way, and what will you do when it does?

cards.advice: A routine sticks when it is repeated at the same cue, so set the time where you actually do it.
cards.action: Change the Behavior's set time to where you keep moving it.

evidence.claim: In a trial with 192 adults, carrying out the plan again and again at its planned cue was a key predictor of the routine becoming automatic.
evidence.quote: Repeated plan enactment was a key predictor for automaticity.

cards.limitation: The trial studied one everyday eating habit over 84 days; schedules with a fixed external constraint may not move.
quip_seeds: You moved {behavior} to near {median_target_time_clock} on {same_direction_days|day|days} of the last {window_days}.
{behavior} keeps landing near {median_target_time_clock}. Setting it there may stick better.

cards.advice: New routines take weeks to months to feel automatic, and the time varies a lot, so the first two weeks are too early to judge one.
cards.action: Keep the same time and place for now rather than changing it early.

evidence.claim: In 82 people building a daily habit, the time to reach most of its automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days.
evidence.quote: The time it took participants to reach 95% of their asymptote of automaticity ranged from 18 to 254 days; indicating considerable variation in how long it takes people to reach their limit of automaticity and highlighting that it can take a very long time.

cards.limitation: One study of simple daily eating, drinking and activity habits; less frequent Behaviors may take longer.
quip_seeds: {behavior}: {completed} done, {not_completed} not done in its first two weeks. Still early to feel automatic, so keep the slot steady.
{behavior} is {age_days|day|days} old. Routines often need weeks more to feel automatic, so it is early to judge it.

cards.advice: Comparing what you did against what you planned, and adjusting, works better than tracking alone.
cards.action: Look at this week on the Behaviors page and adjust one tight spot.

evidence.claim: In 122 evaluations of eating and activity programs, those that paired self-monitoring with goal setting, feedback or review did better than the rest.
evidence.quote: Interventions that combined self-monitoring with at least one other technique derived from control theory were significantly more effective than the other interventions (0.42 vs. 0.26).

cards.limitation: The programs targeted eating and physical activity; other kinds of routines were not studied.

{behavior} this week: {week_rate_pct}, against {prior_rate_pct} usually. Worth a look at what got in the way?

cards.advice: Habits tend to form more reliably at a time and place that stay the same each time the routine comes up.
cards.action: Check what is different on that weekday, then move the Behavior that day or drop it from that day.

evidence.claim: Habit researchers advise repeating an action in a context met every day of the week, so the cue stays the same.
evidence.quote: Be consistent: choose a time and place that you encounter every day of the week.

cards.limitation: Expert advice drawn from habit research and written for daily habits; not a trial of weekday schedules.
quip_seeds: {behavior} on {weekday_name}s: {weekday_rate_pct}, against {other_rate_pct} on other days. What is different then?
{weekday_name}s get done {weekday_rate_pct} of the time, against {other_rate_pct} on other days. What is different about {weekday_name}s?

cards.advice: A steady routine often runs on its cue, so keeping its time and place protects it.
cards.action: Leave this Behavior's time and place unchanged when you rearrange your day.

evidence.claim: Once a habit forms, the setting itself starts the action, without needing a conscious goal each time.
evidence.quote: Once a habit is formed, perception of contexts triggers the associated response without a mediating goal.

cards.limitation: A theory review; it explains why changing the cue can disrupt a habit but does not measure how often it does. Four steady weeks do not always mean a habit has formed.
quip_seeds: {behavior}: {completed} of {resolved} over {weeks|week|weeks}. Keep its time and place steady when you rearrange your day.
{behavior} has held at {rate_pct} for {weeks|week|weeks}. Worth leaving its time and place as they are.

cards.advice: A Not Completed day now and then does not undo a routine; what matters is picking it up the next time.
cards.action: After a Not Completed day, keep the next day's plan as it is.

evidence.claim: In a study of people building daily habits, missing a single day did not noticeably set back habit formation.
evidence.quote: Missing one opportunity to perform the behaviour did not materially affect the habit formation process.

cards.limitation: The study looked at single missed days, not long breaks.
quip_seeds: {behavior}: {completed} of {resolved} over {weeks|week|weeks}. A Not Completed day now and then does not undo it; keep the next day's plan.
{behavior} is at {rate_pct} for {weeks|week|weeks}, with a few Not Completed days. Those do not undo a routine.

cards.advice: When a Behavior rarely gets done, a smaller version can be easier to start and repeat.
cards.action: Shorten it, move it to a better time, or archive it for now.

evidence.claim: Habit researchers advise small, manageable changes, because failure can be discouraging.
evidence.quote: Patients should be encouraged to aim for small and manageable behaviour changes, because failure can be discouraging.

cards.limitation: Expert advice drawn from habit research, written for clinicians; not a trial of shrinking a routine.
quip_seeds: {behavior}: {completed} of {resolved} in {weeks|week|weeks}. A smaller version may be easier to start. Shorten it?
{behavior} is at {rate_pct} for {weeks|week|weeks}. A smaller version, a new time, or archive it for now?

cards.advice: Plan ahead for the weeks that go badly, so getting back is a step you already know.
cards.action: Note in the Behavior's description what helped you get back on track, for the next dip.

evidence.claim: NICE recommends helping people make coping plans to prevent and manage lapses, as part of goals and planning.
evidence.quote: develop coping plans to prevent and manage relapses

cards.limitation: National guidance for health behaviour programs; it recommends the technique rather than testing it in an app.
quip_seeds: {behavior} dipped to {dip_rate_pct} for {dip_weeks|week|weeks} and came back. Note what helped in its description, for next time.
{behavior} is back to {recent_rate_pct} after a dip to {dip_rate_pct}. What helped? Note it in its description.

cards.advice: An Unresolved Occurrence is not a failure; it just has no decision yet.
cards.action: Mark what you remember and leave the rest Unresolved.

evidence.claim: Cadence treats an Unresolved Occurrence as missing a decision, never as Not Completed.
evidence.quote: Unresolved remains missing decision data.

cards.limitation: A Cadence product rule, not research evidence.

{behavior} has {unmarked|past Occurrence|past Occurrences} with no mark. Mark the ones you remember; the rest can stay Unresolved.

cards.advice: Doing a newer routine right after an established one, rather than before it, can help it stick.
cards.action: Keep the newer of the two set right after the other, not before it.

evidence.claim: People told to floss after brushing formed stronger flossing habits than people told to floss before, and still flossed more 8 months later.
evidence.quote: Those who flossed after brushing (rather than before) tended to form stronger flossing habits and, at 8-month follow-up, had stronger habits and flossed more frequently.

cards.limitation: An exploratory study of 50 people and one habit; it compared after with before, not pairing with not pairing.

cards.advice: People tend to underestimate how long tasks take, so several Behaviors set for one hour can crowd each other out.
cards.action: Move one Behavior to a quieter hour, or check that their lengths fit in the hour.

evidence.claim: People's estimates of how long their own tasks would take were too optimistic for many kinds of tasks.
evidence.quote: Ss' predictions of their completion times were too optimistic for a variety of academic and nonacademic tasks.

cards.limitation: The study measured time estimates for student tasks; linking it to a crowded hour is our reading. Your own numbers for that hour matter more.

{behavior} shares {hour_label} with other Behaviors and gets done {hour_rate_pct} of the time there. Move it to a quieter hour?

cards.advice: People underestimate how long their own tasks take, unless they think back to how long it took before.
cards.action: Give each Behavior a length based on how long it took last time, so the day does not overfill.

evidence.claim: People's estimates of how long their own tasks would take were too optimistic, and recalling past times removed the bias.
evidence.quote: The optimistic bias was eliminated for Ss instructed to connect relevant past experiences with their predictions.

cards.limitation: Studied with student projects and tasks, not daily routines.

cards.advice: If sessions keep running longer than planned, plan for the time they actually take.
cards.action: Change the Behavior's length to the time it usually takes.

evidence.claim: People's estimates of how long their own tasks would take were too optimistic, and recalling past times removed the bias.
evidence.quote: The optimistic bias was eliminated for Ss instructed to connect relevant past experiences with their predictions.

cards.limitation: Studied with student projects and tasks, not daily routines.

cards.advice: Repeating a routine at its usual cue helps it become automatic, so keep a Behavior at its usual time when the day allows.
cards.action: When the day allows, leave it at its usual time; if you keep moving it the same way, give it a new usual time.

evidence.claim: In a trial with 192 adults, carrying out the plan again and again at its planned cue was a key predictor of the routine becoming automatic.
evidence.quote: Repeated plan enactment was a key predictor for automaticity.

cards.limitation: Moved days are often already disrupted, so a lower rate on moved days does not show that moving caused it. The trial studied one eating habit.
quip_seeds: {behavior}: {unmoved_rate_pct} done at its usual time, {moved_rate_pct} on moved days. When the day allows, keep it at its usual time.
Left at their usual time, Behaviors got done {unmoved_rate_pct} of the time; moved, {moved_rate_pct}. Keep the usual time when the day allows.

cards.advice: A new routine starts more reliably with a plan for when and where it happens.
cards.action: Set a Where for each new Behavior next to its time; Anywhere is fine for ones that move around.

evidence.claim: Across 94 tests, people who planned when, where and how to act reached their goals more often than people who only intended to.
evidence.quote: Findings from 94 independent tests showed that implementation intentions had a positive effect of medium‐to‐large magnitude ( d = .65) on goal attainment.

cards.limitation: The studies tested full when, where and how plans, not a Where field alone; most were short and many were lab tasks.
quip_seeds: {behaviors_without_place|Behavior has|Behaviors have} a time but no Where yet. Naming where each happens makes it easier to start.
To make new routines easier to start, add a Where to the {behaviors_without_place|Behavior|Behaviors} without one. Anywhere counts too.

cards.advice: Planning many new routines at once can make the load feel harder to keep; starting with a few is easier to hold.
cards.action: Keep the two or three Behaviors that matter most this month, and archive the rest for later.

evidence.claim: Detailed planning helped people with one goal but not with several, because it made the combined load feel hard.
evidence.quote: An investigation into this question suggests that the benefits of implemental planning for attaining a single goal do not typically extend to multiple goals.

cards.limitation: Lab and field experiments with short tasks studied detailed planning across goals; the right number of routines differs from person to person.
quip_seeds: {behaviors_created_last_14_days|new Behavior|new Behaviors} in two weeks is a heavy load to plan at once. Keep the two or three that matter most?
You are starting with {active_behaviors|Behavior|Behaviors}. A few at a time are easier to keep. Archive some for later?

cards.advice: Setting a new Behavior right after something you already do every day gives it a steady starting point.
cards.action: Set each new Behavior's time just after a daily routine, such as breakfast or arriving at work.

evidence.claim: Habit researchers suggest using a cue from an existing daily routine as a stable starting point for a new habit.
evidence.quote: A cue located within an existing daily routine (for example, ‘when I go on my lunch break’) provides a convenient and stable starting point.

cards.limitation: Expert advice drawn from habit research, written for clinicians. A trial found routine cues and clock times worked about equally well, so a clock time alone is fine too.
quip_seeds: For your {active_behaviors|new Behavior|new Behaviors}: setting each just after something you already do daily, like breakfast, gives a steady start.
Is there a daily routine just before each of your {active_behaviors|Behavior|Behaviors}? Setting the time right after it gives a steady start.

cards.advice: Recording what you actually did, Completed or Not Completed, is one of the ingredients most linked to changing a routine.
cards.action: Mark each Behavior Completed or Not Completed once it is done or skipped.

evidence.claim: Across 122 program evaluations, self-monitoring explained more of the difference between programs than any other technique.
evidence.quote: The technique, "self-monitoring," explained the greatest amount of among-study heterogeneity (13%).

cards.limitation: The programs targeted eating and physical activity; the finding is about programs, not individual people.
quip_seeds: {active_behaviors|Behavior|Behaviors} to track. Marking each one Completed or Not Completed is the part research links most to change.
Mark your {active_behaviors|Behavior|Behaviors} Completed or Not Completed; an honest record is the part that helps most.
